passage: Monday. A stranger messaged Tenzin in a game chat. "You are so mature for your age. Not like the other kids." Tenzin felt his cheeks warm and sat a little taller. Wednesday. The stranger wrote again. "Our chats are special. Don't tell anyone, not even your parents." Tenzin's stomach went tight. He remembered a school talk about secrets that make you uneasy. Friday. He stopped replying and told Binita Ma'am, his class teacher, at the end of the day. She stayed with him and said, "This is not your fault. You have done nothing wrong. Thank you for telling me." She told the school safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that evening.

qa.q: On which day did Tenzin tell Binita Ma'am?
What did Tenzin feel on Monday, and what changed by Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt flattered, his cheeks warm and sitting taller; by Wednesday the request to keep it secret made his stomach go tight and uneasy.

qa.q: What should a child do when a stranger flatters them and asks for secrecy?
qa.a: Stop replying and tell a parent or teacher, as Tenzin did with Binita Ma'am 🤍.

qa.q: How might Binita Ma'am see Tenzin's decision to tell her?
qa.a: As a brave and sensible step: she stayed with him, said it was not his fault, told the safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that same evening.

grounding: Illustrates a child flattered by an online stranger who asks for secrecy, recognising the warning and telling a teacher.

passage:
I'm Binita. A few weeks ago, someone in my drawing game started sending me messages. At first they were just nice: "Your art is amazing." Then: "You're so mature, not like other kids. You're special." I felt flattered. Nobody had ever called me mature before.
Then, one morning before school, a message said, "Let's keep our chats secret. Grown-ups won't understand us."
My stomach went cold. A secret from Mummy? I didn't reply. At the first break I told Maria Miss, my voice shaking. She listened to everything, then said, "You have done nothing wrong. Telling me was brave." She called Mummy that same afternoon, and at home we saved the messages, blocked the account and reported it together.
I still draw. I just don't chat with strangers any more.

qa.q: What did the message say grown-ups would not do?
qa.a: It said grown-ups won't understand them.

qa.q: How did Binita's feelings change when the stranger asked for secrecy?
qa.a: Binita went from flattered to frightened; the cold stomach showed that something felt wrong.

qa.q: What did Maria Miss do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, told Binita that nothing was Binita's fault, and called Mummy the same afternoon so the messages were saved, blocked and reported.

qa.q: Why might the stranger have praised Binita so much before asking for secrecy?
qa.a: The praise was meant to make Binita feel special and trusting, so a secret would feel like part of the friendship.

grounding: A child flattered by an online stranger who then asks for secrecy recognises the red flag, stops replying and tells a teacher, who acts that day.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Wednesday
Santosh came to my room at lunch with his friend Jahnavi, who kept a hand on his sleeve and said, "Just tell. It's okay."
Santosh showed me messages on his mother's old phone from someone in a homework-help group: "You're smarter than kids your age." "You're special to me." "Don't tell your parents about our chats, they'll spoil it."
He said he had stopped replying but felt he had done something bad. I told him clearly that he had done nothing wrong and that coming to me was exactly right. We took screenshots together. I phoned his mother before school ended; she came in, and we blocked and reported the account and informed the school's safeguarding lead that afternoon.
When he left, Santosh's shoulders had dropped. Jahnavi walked him back to class.

qa.q: Where did the messages come from?
What was Santosh feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and worried, believing he had done something bad.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day?
qa.a: They told him it was not his fault, took screenshots with him, phoned his mother, blocked and reported the account and informed the safeguarding lead.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi see her friend's situation?
qa.a: Jahnavi could see Santosh needed help, so she encouraged him to speak and stayed close to him.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a boy flattered and asked for secrecy by an online stranger, who stops replying and is told he did nothing wrong.
